data.title: The Federal Reserve resumes interest rate hikes: the end of an era of low interest rates.
data.description: Zhou Hao: For investors, this means that one of the most successful strategies of the past decade—betting on long-term interest rate declines and loose liquidity—may no longer be effective. By Zhou Hao, Chief Economist at GTJAI, a subsidiary of Guotai Haitong Securities. While the market was still immersed in the narrative of "interest rate cuts are inevitable" from the past few years, the Federal Reserve broke this conventional thinking with a 25-basis-point rate hike. On September 16, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. This is the first interest rate hike in over three years, and a formal reversal of the easing cycle expected in 2025. More noteworthy than the rate hike itself is the signal it sends: during the previous easing cycle, growth remained robust, employment remained strong, and inflation was far more sticky than the market anticipated; against this backdrop, not cutting rates, or even raising them, became almost inevitable. In this sense, the Federal Reserve is sending an important message to the market: the era of interest rates returning to pre-pandemic lows may not return. The most intriguing aspect of this meeting is the high degree of consistency between the policy statement and economic forecasts. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh explicitly stated that too many components of inflation have still risen by more than 3% in the past six months to a year. At the same time, the Federal Reserve raised its 2026 core PCE inflation forecast to 3.4% and its overall PCE inflation forecast to 3.7%. This means that after years of fighting inflation, price pressures have not completely disappeared. More importantly, the Federal Reserve did not lower its growth forecasts due to the interest rate hikes. Instead, the committee raised its GDP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 while lowering its unemployment rate forecast. This effectively breaks a core assumption in the traditional monetary policy framework: that interest rate hikes will significantly drag down the economy. At least in the Fed's view, the current US economy is much more resilient to interest rates than in the past. This is also the fundamental reason why the latest dot plot is so hawkish. Sixteen of the 18 policymakers expect further rate hikes this year, and four officials even believe that two more rate hikes are needed. More noteworthy is that the dot plot shows that the median interest rate will remain at 4.125% at the end of 2027, meaning that there is almost no room for rate cuts in the coming year. The market has historically viewed each rate hike as a prelude to the next rate cut, but the Federal Reserve now seems to want to break this conditioned reflex. To some extent, the Fed is undergoing a cognitive reshaping. For over a decade, investors have held a deep-seated belief that the Fed will eventually intervene to rescue the market should the economy slow even slightly. However, the Fed under Warsh has exhibited a drastically different style from its predecessors. Its record-breaking reduction in press conference time reflects its consistent advocacy for less forward guidance and lower policy communication frequency. In other words, the Fed is no longer willing to provide the market with a clear path forward, but rather wants the market to price in data rather than verbal promises from the central bank. This shift implies that financial market volatility may be higher in the long term than it has been in the past decade. The bond market has already begun to react. Following the meeting, the yield on the two-year U.S. Treasury note quickly rose to 4.74%, while the yield on the 10-year Treasury note climbed to 5%, reaching its highest level since 2007. For many investors, the 5% yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note is not just a number, but a dividing line of an era. In the past decade or so of ultra-low interest rates, the global asset pricing system has been built on the premise that the risk-free rate is close to zero. Whether it's the valuation of technology stocks, private equity financing, or real estate capitalization rates, all have benefited from extremely low discount rates. Now, this foundation is being completely rewritten. If the yield on long-term U.S. Treasury bonds can remain stable at around 5%, then many assets will have to be revalued. This is especially crucial for the stock market. This round of interest rate hikes did not occur on the eve of an economic recession, but rather in the middle of an economic expansion cycle. Historical experience shows that mid-cycle rate hikes are often more difficult to manage than those before a recession. This is because corporate profits have not yet deteriorated, but valuations have already begun to be squeezed by higher financing costs and discount rates. The two main forces supporting the rise in US stocks over the past two years were optimistic profit expectations brought about by artificial intelligence and market bets on future easing policies. Now, the second condition is weakening. If interest rates continue to rise while profit growth slows, then valuation expansion will be unsustainable. From this perspective, the real impact of the Fed's rate hikes on the stock market is not a slowdown in growth, but a revaluation of capital costs. At the same time, the US dollar has also received new support. Previously, as some economies in Europe and Japan gradually withdrew from ultra-loose policies, the interest rate differential between the US and other developed economies narrowed, putting pressure on the dollar index. However, as the Fed has turned hawkish again, the interest rate advantage has tilted back towards the dollar. For Asian markets, this could mean a new round of capital outflow pressure. Historical experience shows that once US real interest rates continue to rise, Asian currencies usually face depreciation pressure, and capital tends to flow back to dollar assets. The Japanese yen has become the most direct victim, and other Asian currencies are also finding it difficult to remain unaffected. For Hong Kong, the impact is even more direct. The linked exchange rate system dictates that Hong Kong must follow the US interest rate cycle. When expectations of US interest rate hikes rise, the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar widens, carry trade activities increase, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate faces downward pressure. At the same time, local financing costs, the real estate market, and capital market valuations will continue to be affected. However, if this round of market turmoil is simply understood as a normal monetary policy adjustment, the complexity of the issue may be underestimated. In fact, the Federal Reserve appears so hawkish not only because current inflation data is high, but also because the US economy is undergoing a series of structural changes. First, the forces driving inflation are increasingly coming from the supply side. Neither geopolitical energy price fluctuations nor the expansion of capital expenditures triggered by investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure can easily suppress demand-driven inflation through traditional interest rate hikes. Second, the US fiscal situation is becoming a new macroeconomic constraint. Currently, the US fiscal deficit has long remained around 6% of GDP, and the federal debt continues to expand. The bond market is increasingly focused not only on the Fed's interest rates, but also on the US government's ability to continue financing in the future. In the past, the market generally believed that the risk premium for US Treasury bonds was close to zero. Now, this assumption is changing. The rise in the 10-year US Treasury yield to 5% reflects not only adjustments in short-term monetary policy expectations, but also a reassessment of the sustainability of US fiscal policy by investors. Secondly, the investment boom in artificial intelligence is reshaping the supply and demand relationship in the capital market. To build data centers, computing clusters, and energy infrastructure, large US technology companies are issuing long-term bonds on an unprecedented scale. This increased supply of corporate bonds is, in effect, competing with US Treasury bonds for global capital, pushing up the long-term level of the entire interest rate system. In other words, rising yields come not only from monetary policy but also from capital demand itself. This may mean that the central level of long-term US interest rates will be systematically higher than pre-pandemic levels in the coming years. Therefore, what is truly noteworthy in this round of interest rate hikes is not the widely discussed "how many more rate hikes there will be," but rather the Fed's redefinition of the neutral interest rate. The latest dot plot further raises the median long-term interest rate to 3.25%. This seemingly insignificant adjustment is actually of great significance. It signifies that policymakers are increasingly convinced that the natural interest rate in the US economy has shifted upward. Demographic changes, widening fiscal deficits, investment in energy transition, and the construction of artificial intelligence infrastructure are collectively driving capital demand to remain higher than in the past decade. If this assessment holds true, then global financial markets may be entering a new era: inflation will not return to pre-pandemic ultra-low levels, nor will interest rates. For investors, this means that one of the most successful strategies of the past decade—betting on long-term interest rate declines and loose liquidity—may no longer be effective. The Fed's 25 basis point rate hike appears on the surface to be a routine policy adjustment. However, at a deeper level, it marks a turning point. The US economy needs to adapt to higher financing costs, the US fiscal system faces stricter market constraints, global capital needs to reassess the attractiveness of dollar assets, and emerging markets must re-cope with the cyclical return of a "strong dollar." Therefore, the most important conclusion of this meeting was not that "the Federal Reserve has restarted interest rate hikes," but rather that the market has finally begun to realize that an era of low interest rates that has lasted for more than a decade may have truly come to an end.

data.title: It's time to make Ethereum faster: How the ecosystem views EIP-8198
data.description:
Author: Ethlabs Source: X, @ethlabs_org Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Ethereum has the potential to become faster, and now is the time to make it happen. We visited the entire ecosystem to find out what they really think about EIP-8198 (Quick Slots). This article compiles what we learned from 20 interviewees—who range from DeFi founders, application developers, and infrastructure researchers.

There have been many "Ethereum killers" over the past decade, and one of their main selling points was "Ethereum, but faster."

Despite this, Ethereum L1, together with its various L2 layers, remains the largest DeFi ecosystem: as of September 17, 2026, the total value locked has exceeded $58 billion; and the total trading volume of spot DEXs across all layers this year has exceeded $750 billion. Amid this growth, Ethereum L1 has maintained a restrained approach to speed improvements: speed is important, but not at the expense of censorship resistance, decentralization, and trust neutrality—the very foundation of Ethereum's value. This approach has earned Ethereum widespread trust as the preferred on-chain store of value. Now, we believe there is an opportunity to make Ethereum even faster while strengthening these core characteristics. EIP-8198 Arrives! Ethereum currently produces blocks every 12 seconds. With EIP-8198 (also known as "Quick Slots"), we can begin to reduce this time. @CarlBeek wrote this EIP in March of this year, and @barnabemonnot brought it to the Ethereum Core Developers Conference (ACD) on August 6th, proposing its inclusion in the Hegotá upgrade. Progress has been made since then, receiving feedback from @fradamt and an increasing number of ecosystem and client teams. This EIP consists of two parts: A larger, one-time refactoring to remove the assumptions about a fixed block order in the Ethereum software. Using the results of this refactoring, the block time will be gradually increased. The first step is to reduce the block interval from 12 seconds to 10 seconds; further reductions will be evaluated separately once the network is ready. Each subsequent reduction will still need to be tested and validated through consensus, but the underlying work supporting these adjustments will be in place by then. The path to a faster Ethereum begins with making Ethereum's block time easier and safer to modify—this is the core idea of ​​Quick Slots. Ethereum has long adopted this gradual approach to scaling: as the network shows more capacity, the gas cap is gradually increased; as data capacity improves, blob capacity can also be reassessed. We believe latency issues deserve the same treatment. Who cares? We don't believe Ethereum L1 must become the world's fastest trading platform to be valuable. But we believe that an Ethereum L1 that continues to serve as a secure and decentralized settlement layer for the global economy can become even faster. To put it bluntly: a faster Ethereum means a smoother Ethereum, and that's intuitively true. Shorter wait times mean a better user experience. However, our conversations with various builders within the ecosystem reveal that the benefits go far beyond that. Here are some of the findings we've learned: Faster block generation makes Ethereum's market more efficient. Ethereum L1 itself is already a significant market: in just the past 30 days, it processed approximately $41.25 billion in DEX trading volume. For comparison, the Singapore Stock Exchange's securities trading volume in August 2026 was approximately $33.9 billion. Continuous improvements to the L1 protocol speed will further enhance this type of activity, making Ethereum a truly globally competitive value settlement layer and bringing more and more people into centralized finance. The market doesn't wait for Ethereum blocks. Prices are constantly moving, and demand changes between adjacent blocks. Shorter slots allow for more frequent on-chain liquidity updates, thus shortening the time window for prices to become stale, leading to better transactions for users and creating better conditions for liquidity providers. @DefiLlama founder @0xngmi explained what faster slots might mean for users of their product, LlamaSwap. LlamaSwap is a real-time exchange aggregator that compares quotes from various DEXs: "Faster slots improve the trading experience because smaller price fluctuations between blocks allow for much tighter slippage." Austin Adams (@aadams), founder of @dopplerprotocol, a project focused on asset issuance and liquidity launch on Ethereum, sees the same improvement from the perspective of liquidity providers: "Faster block times on Ethereum directly improve LP returns, making capital markets more efficient. The rapid implementation of EIP-8198 helps ensure that the network remains the dominant venue for capital formation and trading." According to crypto options platform @DeriveXYZ, these benefits span multiple markets. Josh Kim (@josh_pwrk), the project lead, pointed out that waiting for an L1 trade exposes arbitrageurs to price risk, affecting their ability to rebalance the Derive market and maintain narrow spreads. Note: Derive V3 will be deployed on Ethereum L1. "Large options trades on Derive often drive our perpetual and spot markets on our DEX, and arbitrageurs are key players in rebalancing the market. The faster block times on L1 directly impact how much commission, slippage, and risk arbitrageurs bear. For example, in a long spot/short perpetual arbitrage trade, the trader bears 12 seconds of price risk while waiting for the spot trade to settle on L1, forcing them to only enter during periods of significant price volatility." The benefits of Quick Slots also extend to tokenized stocks and ETFs. @Ondo completes subscriptions and redemptions via RFQ: the price is signed off-chain, and the user's transaction must then be posted on Ethereum. During the waiting period, the underlying asset continues to trade; therefore, shorter slots reduce this risk exposure and give the quoting party more room to narrow the price spread. Armand Khatri (@armandkhatri), Head of the Ondo Ecosystem, tells us: "For tokenized stocks and ETFs, the market that determines the price never waits for Ethereum to produce a block. Every second between a quote signing and transaction confirmation carries price risk that someone has to bear, and this risk is ultimately reflected in the price difference. Shorter slots narrow this window, bringing on-chain prices closer to off-chain reference prices. This is a real improvement, and it doesn't require Ethereum to give up any of its features that make it worthy of being used as a settlement layer." At the institutional level, Ethereum Institutional (@ethereuminsti) co-founder @ismiMatthew believes that Ethereum's ability to sense the market is part of its growing appeal to financial institutions. "As more and more institutional activities move onto the blockchain, these improvements make Ethereum increasingly compelling as a financial market infrastructure. They also strengthen market confidence—that Ethereum is capable of delivering on its phased roadmap and continuously raising the bar for technical standards." PropellerHeads (@PropellerSwap) founder @Haikane mentioned the rise of trading on Ethereum and discussed how reducing latency can improve profit margins, thus making L1 the ideal platform for more businesses to migrate and trade assets. "Competition in trading businesses is built on extremely thin profit margins, so even relatively small improvements in latency can be significant." Aerodrome (@aeroxyz) contributor @ZoomerAnon believes that faster block generation can bring better prices to traders, reduce losses from arbitrageurs, and keep more trading activity in on-chain liquidity pools. Note: Aerodrome is currently creating instances on Ethereum L1. "We definitely support faster block times. Like other DEXs that carry liquidity, faster block times allow us to get more up-to-date prices for traders and reduce the value taken by arbitrageurs. I don't think it's in Ethereum's interest to have a large number of transactions completed through centralized market makers, which is, to some extent, a result of slow block times. Our protocol can easily adjust parameters and replace modules to adapt to faster or newer block times, and fortunately, we don't need to redeploy when block times change." These teams approach the problem from different angles, but they all point to the same thing: shorter block times mean more frequent Ethereum state updates, which means that people trading on L1 can enjoy a more efficient market. If Ethereum can provide updated states without sacrificing the trustworthy decentralization attributes that make markets credible, then this is an improvement worth pursuing—because it directly supports Ethereum continuing to serve as the core hub for applications and their users building decentralized markets. For users, a faster Ethereum is a better Ethereum. One way to understand the value of this EIP is to look at users who aren't even thinking about slots (at least not the kind of slots we're discussing here). FWA.fun, built by @token_works, has recently become one of the Ethereum gas-consuming applications, bringing a batch of new users directly to L1 and bringing back many people who haven't used the mainnet for a long time. TokenWorks founder Adam (@Rhynotic) shared a consumer-level application perspective—its users will directly experience the Ethereum L1 waiting time. "Faster block times are a huge help for FWA for several reasons: First, users don't like waiting, even if you try to hide the waiting as much as possible in the front end; second, the Chainlink VRF used by FWA currently adds a 3-block confirmation delay, so shorter block times mean less waiting time for the entire system. Many of our users repeatedly buy/initiate transactions, so every second saved counts." Regarding additional notes on confirmation delays: Another part of our "Faster Ethereum" workflow, FCR, can reduce confirmation time by 30 times, which also helps solve this problem. For Railgun (@RAILGUN_Project), the potential benefits also extend to privacy. Contributor Dan Lipert (@dan_lipert) believes that faster block generation brings more liquidity to L1, supports a larger privacy set, and gives compliance tools more opportunities to respond when users interact with applications. "Faster Ethereum block generation means more concentrated liquidity on L1, which means more privacy through a larger privacy set. Compliance tools also have more opportunities to react in truly important time windows, resulting in a smoother overall experience that allows Railgun users to use all the tools and platforms they want privately without waiting." If we can make interacting with Ethereum L1 feel faster without making Ethereum less Ethereum, it's a better Ethereum experience for everyone who gets involved with the mainnet. Note: Ethereum L2 has long been optimized for much faster interactions, but L1 performs a different task: it provides a highly secure, trustworthy, neutral, and censorship-resistant settlement layer that systems can ultimately rely on. For builders like Adam and Dan who want to make user-facing products more closely aligned with these characteristics, a faster Ethereum is undoubtedly helpful. Faster also means better censorship resistance. A major motivation for people to transact on decentralized blockchains is censorship resistance—the cornerstone of a truly free market. If someone refuses to process your transaction, Ethereum should provide you with an alternative channel as quickly as possible. George Davies (@_eltitan), the engineering lead at Gattaca (@gattacahq), the team that created Titan Builder—which now produces about half of Ethereum's blocks—is looking at Quick Slots from this perspective: "In our view, this is the number one priority for the next major consensus layer EIP. I think it's the biggest unlocking for DeFi users in terms of experience, while also bringing benefits in terms of censorship resistance and finality." For someone under censorship, block time is equivalent to waiting time—it determines how long they have to wait for the next transaction to be packaged. This is especially interesting when compared to Hegotá's signature EIP—FOCIL. FOCIL gives an additional role to a committee of validators (called the includer) in transaction packaging, while Quick Slots increase the frequency of these packaging opportunities. With a 12-second block time, Ethereum schedules five opportunities per minute; with 10 seconds, it becomes six. Essentially, FOCIL opens more doors for censored transactions to enter Ethereum, while Quick Slots make those doors appear more frequently. Michael Mosier (@mostlyblocks), Head of Research at @blockspace_eth, also emphasized the quality of transaction packaging: "Shorter slots should be the highest priority because they improve the quality of block space through faster, more predictable packaging. This stimulates user activity and benefits the network and the infrastructure that serves the network." Patrick Apriori (@apriori0x) from Frachtis VC (@frachtisvc), host of the Credible Commitments podcast (which recently discussed Quick Slots!), took this argument a step further: "Quick Slots bring better censorship resistance, improving all mainnet applications and L2..." The bridge's user experience makes Ethereum more attractive as a global financial value settlement layer. In conjunction with FOCIL, Quick Slots make censorship more expensive, shorter, and structurally more difficult to implement. This leads to another useful concept: economic censorship resistance—the cost to an adversary to block a transaction off-chain. Shorter slots mean users wait less for the next block production opportunity, while adversaries attempting continuous censorship over a fixed period face more block producer opportunities. FOCIL adds an additional includeer to this process. Performance and resilience are usually inversely related, but with Quick Slots, they can move in tandem. A settlement layer serving the world should be difficult to censor and able to recover quickly if someone attempts to censor it. Quick Slots can make Ethereum faster without jeopardizing its core features. Of course, faster block generation is only truly important if it doesn't compromise the decentralization that gives L1 its value. Burak (@boez95) and colleagues at Flashbots have specifically researched this issue and publicly released their evaluation of Quick Slots. Their conclusion is supportive: "We support this direction. Shorter slots can reduce confirmation latency and potentially improve user experience… Therefore, we support making slot timing configurable and gradually experimenting with shorter slots." More importantly, Flashbots examined how shorter slots would affect geographical decentralization. Shorter slots compress the available time for the entire block production process, potentially putting participants located far from major network and infrastructure hubs at a disadvantage. However, their latency-calibrated simulations show that this is unlikely to be a substantial constraint at the currently discussed slot times. Even reducing slot times from 12 seconds to 6 seconds, while regional revenue disparities widened, the results regarding geographical concentration remained largely unchanged. Their conclusion is that geographical factors are more of a potential upper limit on how low slot times can ultimately be reduced without creating additional centralized pressure, rather than a current constraint, than the extent of the reduction currently being considered. At Ethlabs, we are also closely tracking the propagation time of all nodes across the network to better understand the impact of Quick Slots. This is particularly important because Ethereum is looking towards post-quantum migration and how future consensus design, shorter slots, and larger post-quantum signatures will relate. Faster Ethereum L1 allows for better coordination among L2 instances. Every L2 instance that relies on Ethereum has interactions that inherit the L1 clock. The simplest example is depositing. Transferring assets or messages from Ethereum L1 to L2 requires an L1 transaction to be packaged; therefore, shorter L1 blocks mean the journey can begin earlier—regardless of whether the L2 instance itself uses Ethereum as its ordering layer. For some interoperability designs, the benefits go even further. Armagan (@epochzer0) from The Ethereum Economic Zone (@etheconomiczone) provides a concrete example. EEZ is researching a design that would allow a contract on one rollup to call a contract on another rollup and use its return value within the same transaction. In this design, this synchronization opportunity would be activated at most once per Ethereum L1 block. That is, a 12-second L1 clock would become part of the cross-rollup user experience. "EEZ's design goal is to allow a contract on one rollup to call a contract on another rollup and use the return value in the same transaction. However, this synchronization window is only opened once per L1 slot because everything must be settled within a single L1 block. This means that the L1 slot duration sets the pace of cross-chain collaboration; shorter slots directly multiply the number of times applications can obtain synchronization windows and shorten the worst-case waiting time for the next window. Quick Slots have a dual benefit for EEZ: first, this initial shortening means that synchronization windows will come significantly more frequently; second, making the slot duration adjustable means that every future data-supported shortening will directly translate into a faster cross-rollup collaboration experience for EEZ users." Faster L1 makes collaboration more frequent throughout the Ethereum ecosystem, which also points to the Ethereum L1 we see. The role to be played: A global settlement layer providing an exceptionally secure and decentralized foundation upon which numerous assets, applications, and L2 can rely. A settlement layer that better coordinates the systems that settle on it is more valuable to every participant. Quick Slots is not about making L1 so fast that L2 becomes redundant, but about gradually speeding up the Ethereum mainnet, thereby making L1 stronger along with various types of L2. More voices from the ecosystem: The Ethereum ecosystem is much broader than our timeline suggests, but we hope to hear more feedback from the teams, both positive and negative! Here are more comments from industry leaders:

Greg Casegamas of Lido (@LidoFinance) focuses on Ethereum's broader competitive advantages.

We've already spent a lot of time talking about how helpful Quick Slots is, and you're probably thinking, "Okay, that's great, but what are you doing to make it actually happen?"

Ethlabs uses Quick Slots as a core workflow within our larger "Faster Ethereum" initiative, but like any EIP, it's a network-wide coordinated effort, and we're fortunate to be a part of it. The teams mentioned above, along with many others, are contributing research, implementation, testing, feedback, and support, driving Quick Slots toward readiness. We'll continue to gather these arguments to provide a balanced and comprehensive perspective on why the network, ecosystem, clients, and users might benefit from a faster Ethereum.

data.title: Warsh Rate Hike: Why Didn't Trump Turn Against Him?
data.description:
The first real policy clash between the Federal Reserve and the White House in three years ended with a surprisingly calm response. The Fed announced its first interest rate hike in three years on Wednesday, but Trump's response was unusually mild. This contrasts sharply with his months-long attacks on the Fed's interest rate policy and is the most direct manifestation of Fed Chairman Warsh's efforts to reshape the relationship between the central bank and the White House since taking office in May. Instead of launching an offensive, Trump portrayed himself as the one who proactively "gave way," claiming that after speaking with Warsh beforehand, he said, "You might as well vote with the committee, because the result won't be any different." Behind this rare situation lies a far closer personal relationship between Warsh and Trump than that between Warsh and his predecessor, Powell. According to Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal, Trump proactively called Warsh days before the Federal Reserve meeting, and the conversation extended from private pleasantries to expectations of interest rate hikes. Inside the Ned private club in Washington, several government officials watched Trump's remarks on their phones that evening and were visibly relieved that he hadn't publicly criticized Warsh. However, doubts remain about whether this fragile balance can be sustained, both in the market and among policymakers.

Phone Call: Reconciliation or Intervention

According to a senior White House official, Trump contacted Warsh a few days before the Federal Reserve meeting. The call initially began in a friendly, nostalgic manner, but then shifted to expectations of interest rate hikes.

This call was previously unknown to many of the president's core advisors—some senior officials only learned of it when Trump mentioned it to the media in North Carolina on Wednesday.

The existence of this call was originally unknown to many of the president's core advisors—some senior officials only learned of it when Trump mentioned it to the media in North Carolina on Wednesday.

Trump subsequently characterized the rate hike publicly as a "rate hike targeting Trump," portraying himself as someone who knew he couldn't stop it but acquiesced, claiming Warsh faced a "very tough, anti-White House" committee. Warsh himself refused to discuss any conversations with Trump at the press conference. He characterized the rate hike as the result of the Federal Reserve's own deliberations, calling it "a prudent, serious, and responsible decision that I have been preparing for and considering since taking office in May." He emphasized that his decision was based on economic conditions, not political pressure. White House spokesman Kush Desai stated that Trump "repeatedly reaffirmed his trust in Warsh" while reserving the right to comment on policy. Relationship Management: Warsh's Strategy and Powell's Lessons Learned Compared to his predecessor Powell, Warsh chose a drastically different path. According to those who had contact with Warsh, he was confident in his ability to act according to economic needs while managing his relationship with the president in a way that avoided direct confrontation. He deliberately avoided any statements that might drag the government into the internal disputes of the Federal Reserve, and positioned central bank independence as a principle that needed to be "put into practice rather than publicly declared." This contrasts with Powell's situation. His honeymoon period after the Fed's first rate hike in 2018 lasted only about five months, after which Trump's attacks escalated. While Powell answered the president's calls, he maintained a distant attitude, neither actively maintaining the relationship nor acting as Trump's economic advisor. Trump interpreted this as a confrontational stance. Former Federal Reserve advisor and current Duke University professor Ellen Meade believes that in the current environment, maintaining the Fed's independence may require "managing the president" rather than "distancing oneself from him." She stated that informing the White House of unfavorable news in advance, and avoiding Trump's "immediate outburst" after the policy announcement, could be a feasible strategy. However, she also drew a clear line: providing advance notice is one thing, actively seeking the president's "approval" is another, the latter fundamentally undermining the central bank's independence. She also admitted, "I don't think Warsh can do this job the way Powell does." Historical Precedent: The Greenspan Model and Its Risks Warsh's path is not without historical precedent. Former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan served four administrations, maintaining close relationships with each president and their advisors while maintaining independent policy judgment. In 1992, he broke with the Bush administration—the latter publicly criticized the Fed for its slow pace of interest rate cuts and partly blamed Greenspan for his re-election defeat, famously stating, "I reappointed him, and he disappointed me." However, Warsh's situation carries additional political risks. Former Fed advisor Meade warned that if the White House perceives the interest rate hikes as "imposed" on Warsh rather than a decision he initiated, it could encourage further pressure on other Fed officials. The Trump administration attempted to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook last year, though the Supreme Court blocked the attempt this summer. However, reports indicate the White House has recently taken steps to prepare for another attempt. Some Federal Reserve insiders are also uneasy about the upcoming report on the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, fearing its conclusions will be used by the White House as grounds for firing former Vice Chairman for Supervision Michael Barr. Disagreements remain: Warsh's leadership is questioned. Even without a direct attack from Trump, Warsh still faces criticism from within the president's inner circle. In an interview, Trump's trade advisor Peter Navarro stated that he "tried to understand why Warsh would make such a decision that defied historical precedent and fundamental economic logic."
